experiments.name: C3 gate, run 1 (9 um base chain fidelity, as first declared)
experiments.question: Does our 9 um render plus the official base ink model, with mirror test-time augmentation, reproduce the organizer surface volume and the organizer pixel AUC bars on labelled papyrus?
experiments.method: Official renderer on an organizer mesh of a base-trained segment; pixel AUC of the base ink map against organizer human labels in both depth orders; bars and a VOID clause declared before any data.
experiments.public_summary: The render reproduced the organizer surface volume almost exactly (pooled Pearson 0.9999990). The declared AUC definition did not match the one the bars were set on: under it, even the organizers' own map scored 0.9807 against a 0.987 bar. The run was voided under its own clause and re-declared once.
experiments.lesson: Reproduce the reference archive's own numbers under your metric before declaring bars. A bar copied from one metric definition and applied to another voids the test.

experiments.name: C3-R1: base chain with mirror TTA on a fresh crop

experiments.method: Same chain as run 1. The crop was chosen by hashed code before any map of it existed. AUC was computed inside the organizer supervision mask, both orders, and re-derived by a fresh auditor.

experiments.name: HANDED-1: reader handedness test (coverage-chosen windows)
experiments.question: Can blind readers tell which of a pair of reference-map images is mirror-reversed, so that the reading orientation can be fixed?
experiments.method: Pairs of an official reference map and its mirror image, sides randomised, 3 fresh readers, votes counted by hashed code.
experiments.public_summary: All 12 answers were 'unsure' and no letters were named, so the test was AMBIGUOUS. The windows had been chosen by map coverage alone and may have held no writing.
experiments.lesson: A perception test needs material known to contain the thing perceived.

experiments.public_summary: The decided votes leaned 7:1 toward one state, but the 10-of-12 bar was not met (AMBIGUOUS), so both mirror states stayed as separate reading arms.

experiments.name: D1 sealed benchmark construction
experiments.question: Can a blind picker and three blind sealers build a hash-committed letter seal from official reference maps of held-out text, with confirmed blank windows, before any project render exists?

experiments.public_summary: Three sealed-output sealers produced a consensus seal of 20 letters (9 firm) over five held-out windows from the organizers' official reference maps. experiments.lesson: A seal made by readers measures what readers perceive, not ground truth. Recall against it is a consistency measure.

experiments.question: Can the calibrated reader recover the sealed letters from the official 2.4 um reference maps, and how fast does that fall with blur (sigma_crit)?
experiments.method: Reference maps blurred at 0, 0.15, 0.30 and 0.45 mm, 3 fresh readers per level, positive canary and blank per session, hashed scorer with 5000 permutations.

experiments.name: Geometric handedness rule (sib-handed)
experiments.question: Can the reading orientation (mirror state) of a rendered segment be decided from mesh geometry and scan metadata alone, without readers?
experiments.method: Synthetic spiral scrolls with planted glyphs in proper and reflected frames, then real meshes, metadata and CT-mask centroids only. No image or ink map was viewed.
experiments.public_summary: A rule based on mesh chirality times metadata frame parity reads planted synthetic glyphs correctly in 32/32 cases and mirrors them in 32/32 wrong-sign controls. It is consistent with all organizer affines and with the known-text scroll's winding sense, and it predicted that the orientation shown in the reader tests was the legible one, although those readers had voted at chance. It was packaged as an open tool and proposed as a declaration, but was not adopted as one in the record.
experiments.lesson: Settle orientation from geometry and metadata. Asking LLM readers to judge mirror state was not a reliable instrument.

experiments.name: Tribunal: planted-fault pre-read gate (sib-tribunal)
experiments.question: Can code catch render faults (offset, swapped depth, mirror, off-by-one slice, re-trace by a training segment, wrong voxel size) before any reader sees an image, without false alarms?
experiments.method: Independent reference render of the declared window compared against the delivered stack; one content check per fault type; pre-registered real-data calibration on non-eligible renders.
experiments.public_summary: The gate caught every planted fault by its own check, on synthetic worlds and on real 9 um CT renders, with no clean false alarms. It found that the declared same-papyrus rule missed most true re-traces at the official mesh step, and the project adopted a corrected fail-closed rule. Thresholds stayed proposed, not declared, and at 2.4 um the clean margins were too thin (minimum ratio 1.147, goal 3).
experiments.lesson: Plant the faults you fear and confirm that code catches them. A pre-registered threshold rule can itself be defective, and thresholds calibrated at one voxel size do not transfer to another.

families.summary: This family asked whether blind AI readers can read ink maps of carbonized papyrus, and whether their reads can be trusted. The 9 um base-map chain passed its fidelity gate only on the fourth declared run (one VOID for a metric mismatch, one FAIL with mirror test-time augmentation, one VOID for a freshness breach). Without help, readers named almost nothing on reference maps. With a font key sheet, the readers agreed beyond a shuffle null, and the pre-specified arm replicated once on fresh papyrus. Even so, they never marked an agreed letter as firm, and in three handedness tests they could not tell mirrored maps from normal ones. On a sealed held-out benchmark, the calibrated reader recovered 80 % of the sealed letters from the organizers' 2.4 um reference maps but named nothing at all in the project's own 9 um base or raw maps, so D1 failed. The family also produced tools (the D1 sealed benchmark, a geometric handedness rule, a planted-fault pre-read gate), plus two programmes that were built but never run; the local and remote blind-reader harnesses are listed under Tools, infrastructure and operations.

experiments.name: D3 fold-0841 fine-tune (four arms, sealed reads)
experiments.question: Does a short CPU fine-tune of the public 9 um ink model on nearby PHerc0841 papyrus make unseen 0841 text nameable by blind readers?
experiments.method: Four paired arms started from the same base checkpoint: fine-tune, label-deranged null, depth-reversed, and replay-only control. The fine-tune, null and depth-reversed arms trained 2000 CPU steps on a 288-tile pool (half of each batch, kept at least 128 voxels from five sealed known-text windows) plus replay; the replay-only control trained 2000 steps on replay papyrus only. 24 sealed blind reads were scored by pre-hashed code against pre-registered bars, and an independent audit followed.
experiments.public_summary: This pre-registered test asked whether fine-tuning the public 9 um ink model on 288 tiles of nearby papyrus from the same scroll makes unseen text legible. Verdict: not passed. In all 24 sealed blind reads, every arm (fine-tune, label-scrambled null, depth-reversed control, replay-only control) scored 0 net letters on the sealed known-text windows, with p_max 1. Every reader named 3-13 letters on a known-text canary, so the readers could read. An independent audit re-derived all 144 scored records with 0 mismatches.
experiments.lesson: A small in-domain fine-tune cannot rescue maps that are illegible at 9 um. A known-text canary in every reading session separates 'the reader failed' from 'the map carries nothing'. Teacher labels taken from reference maps agreed only moderately with human labels (kappa 0.61), which caps what such fine-tunes can learn.

experiments.name: Master 8.64 um ink model from scratch (federated CPU training)
experiments.question: Can a 3-D U-Net with fixed 3-D edge channels, trained from scratch on CPU with organizer high-resolution predictions as pseudo-labels at 8.64 um, generalize to a held-out scroll at the same scan setting?
experiments.method: Trained on 18 PHerc0009B segments, with PHerc0343P (8 segments) held out entirely. 12 federated CPU lanes ran 2 fp32 epochs per round and were averaged. Bars were declared before any training data existed: held-out pixel AUC >= 0.90, AP >= 0.50, tile AUC >= 0.85.
experiments.public_summary: Failed its bars. On the held-out scroll (600 crops), the averaged model scored pixel AUC 0.5793, AP 0.1667 and tile AUC 0.575 after round 1, and 0.5778 after round 2, against bars of 0.90, 0.50 and 0.85. The lanes reported 0.63-0.68 on their own validation, so the gain did not transfer. The self-supervised and centralized-control lanes produced no committed result before the fleet ran out of usage credits.
experiments.lesson: Validation on the training scroll overstated transfer. A from-scratch CPU model after two rounds sits far below public pretrained weights on the same held-out crops, so a pipeline should start from the strongest public model.

experiments.name: Fine-tune of a public dense 9 um model on 8.64 um pseudo-labels
experiments.question: Does fine-tuning the decoder and head of the strongest public 9 um model on the same pseudo-labels raise its held-out score at the 8.64 um setting?
experiments.method: Encoder frozen. Decoder and head trained for 2000 steps, batch 4, AdamW lr 1e-4, Dice+BCE on PHerc0009B pseudo-labels. Held-out evaluation every 250 steps on PHerc0343P, keeping the best checkpoint. Bars unchanged from the master-model declaration.
experiments.public_summary: No gain. Fine-tuning only the decoder and head of a public dense 9 um model for 2000 steps on the same pseudo-labels never beat its own starting weights on the held-out scroll: pixel AUC 0.698 at step 0 on isolated crops, 0.634-0.676 at later steps. The kept model is therefore the unchanged public model. Its full-map score (AUC 0.760, AP 0.408, tile AUC 0.688) also misses the 0.90 / 0.50 / 0.85 bars.
experiments.lesson: Fine-tuning on pseudo-labels produced by another model can pull a stronger model toward the labeller's errors. Evaluate step 0 first, and keep the base if no step beats it.

experiments.question: How well do existing public ink models score against the organizer pseudo-labels on the held-out PHerc0343P segment, as a reference for the master-model bars?
experiments.method: Each public model was run with its own documented recipe on the same 600 held-out crops, in both depth orders, and scored with the same pixel AUC, AP and tile-AUC code.
experiments.public_summary: Reference measurement for the master-model bars on 600 held-out crops. The public dense 9 um model scored pixel AUC 0.7605 in forward depth order (0.7694 averaging depth windows), Hecate 9.6 um 0.7309, a public 8 um model 0.7499 per crop, and the base ink_9um model 0.6539. Reverse depth orders scored 0.5352-0.5847 for the main variants. No public model reaches the declared 0.90 bar against these pseudo-labels.
experiments.lesson: Score depth order explicitly, because the wrong order drops every model toward chance. Pseudo-labels from another model also cap any held-out AUC, so the bar must be set against that ceiling.

experiments.name: Pooled-training CPU trainer (D2 infrastructure)
experiments.question: Can a deterministic, resumable CPU trainer be built for the pooled 9 um -> 2.4 um training programme, and what would the programme cost on CPU?
experiments.method: The trainer generalized the D3 fine-tune loop. On synthetic data only, it was tested for bitwise equivalence with the D3 loop, determinism, paired sampling, and resume from checkpoint shards pushed to and fetched from a remote ref. Throughput was measured per tile size and precision.
experiments.public_summary: A reproducible CPU trainer was built and tested on synthetic data only. It matched the earlier fine-tune loop bitwise, was bitwise deterministic, and resumed bitwise from checkpoint shards stored remotely (26 tests passed). experiments.lesson: Measure throughput before committing to a training programme. Remote checkpoint shards make long CPU runs survive container reclaims, at the cost of unreachable objects piling up on the remote.

families.summary: From 30 Sep to 3 Oct 2026, Dominion ran an all-out First Letters screen over the 22 eligible volumes. One or two worker lanes per scroll grew surfaces and ran the official 9 um ink model. The resulting 2 x 2 cm tiles and 4 x 4 cm stitched windows went to blind LLM readers, behind a positive control on held-out known text. Registration mostly worked. experiments.name: flatcheck: flattening-quality checker
experiments.question: Can a per-quad isometry check show where official tifxyz flattenings distort, fold over or collapse, and do SLIM and ARAP do better than the official ABF++?
experiments.method: Per-quad checks (length kept within +-5 %, fold-overs, area and angle distortion, collapse) plus SLIM/ARAP re-flattening. Run on public organizer meshes of a known-text scroll and compared with the official ABF++ on identical triangles. Released as an MIT package with 21 tests on synthetic geometry.
experiments.public_summary: Published as a standalone MIT tool. A clean-clone install passed 21/21 tests and the leak scrub was clean. On the 10 hardest 4 cm2 windows from 38 public meshes of a known-text scroll, the official ABF++ met the 93.1 % reference bar in 0/10 windows, SLIM in 3/10 and ARAP in 4/10. SLIM was at least as good as ABF++ in 33 of 33 comparisons, 8 of them ties. ABF++ collapsed on some meshes (27.9 % of quads within +-5 % after a x2.58 rescale); SLIM never did. The grid flattening as distributed scored 90.1-92.9 % on three whole meshes. The entry was submitted by hand to the September 2026 Progress Prize, because the form needs a signed-in account. No award outcome is recorded.
experiments.lesson: Gentle patches do not separate flattening methods: the unflattened grid already scores 97-99 % there. Test on the most curved and least isometric windows. Report a reference bar as a parameter, not as a validated readability threshold.

experiments.name: handcheck: mirror/handedness predictor
experiments.question: Can mesh geometry plus catalogue metadata predict, before rendering, whether a tifxyz render will read mirrored, and flag meshes that cannot be decided?
experiments.method: The mesh chirality, sign(det[dP/du, dP/dv, r_out]), is multiplied by the catalogue frame parity. Independent centre sources are cross-checked, and a CT frame check tests whether mesh vertices fall on masked-out CT. Validated on planted synthetic glyph renders with a wrong-sign control. Released with 94 tests.
experiments.public_summary: Published as a standalone MIT tool: a clean install passed 94 tests with 1 skipped, and the scrub was clean. Every decided public organizer mesh reads unmirrored as stored, including all 38 meshes of a known-text scroll at HIGH confidence. An independent winding-sense check agreed with the catalogue up/down flag on 36/36 checked meshes. The frame check found that 10 of 15 organizer meshes of one scroll lie 41-91 % on masked-out CT, against at most 3.6 % for every control mesh. These are reported as flags for the organizers, not as established errors. In planted-glyph validation 32/32 renders read unmirrored (min NCC 0.954), and the wrong-sign control came out mirrored 32/32. The brief said 9 of 15 meshes on that scroll were flagged; rerun from public data, the packaged rule flags 11 of 15, and the packager published the rerun number. Reported by the owner as submitted by hand for September (not in the submissions log); no award outcome is recorded.
experiments.lesson: A handedness check means something only if the mesh actually sits on the scroll in its declared frame. Without a frame test, off-scan meshes pass silently. Publish numbers from the packaged rule rerun on public data, not from an earlier internal rule.

experiments.name: tifxyz-dist: certified surface clearance
experiments.question: Can exact point-to-surface distances and certified mesh-to-mesh clearance bounds replace unreliable nearest-vertex checks for train/prediction overlap?
experiments.method: An exact point-to-triangle kernel with pruning, plus certified [lower, upper] mesh-to-mesh bounds with a witness point and a PASS/FAIL certificate at a chosen margin. Checked against an independent kernel and against brute force. Demonstrated on manual vs auto-grown pairs of public segment meshes from an already-read scroll.
experiments.public_summary: Published as a standalone MIT tool: 25/25 tests pass on a clean clone, and the scrub was clean. For a point 1 voxel above a sheet meshed on a 20-voxel grid, the nearest-vertex distance can be off by up to 13.1 voxels; the exact method's error is 0.0. The kernel matches an independent implementation to 2.1e-14, and pruning matches brute force exactly on 4,000 queries. Of 100,000 points sampled on a real 385k-quad segment, none returned a distance above 2.7e-12 voxel. The public demo certified 243 of 396 manual x auto-grown segment pairs. At a 20-voxel margin, 225 passed, 18 failed and 0 were inconclusive. One manual segment touches all 9 auto-grown segments. Several claims on the submission sheet were corrected to match the packaged numbers before submission. Reported by the owner as submitted by hand for September (not in the submissions log); no award outcome is recorded.
experiments.lesson: Nearest-vertex distances on coarse meshes are not a valid contamination test: true re-traces and touching sheets can look several voxels apart. Use point-to-surface distances with certified bounds, and freeze a demo subset rather than waiting for the full set of pairs.

experiments.name: Progress Prize submission path
experiments.question: Can the agent itself submit a verified tool to the monthly Progress Prize form, with every number checked against the published repo?
experiments.method: An entry was marked READY only if: the public repo was re-cloned; tests passed in a clean environment; the leak scrub was clean; the citation and licence rules were met; and the README supported every number. A submission script checked the live form fields and POSTed the entry.
experiments.public_summary: All three September packages passed the automated release checks: install, tests, citation, licences, AI disclosure and zero scrub hits. Automated submission failed twice. First, the agent's own safety check refused the form POST as a real-world transaction. After the owner granted permission, the form endpoint returned HTTP 401, because it accepts only signed-in accounts. The entry was not retried, and the owner submitted by hand from a prepared sheet. The submissions log confirms one hand submission. The owner reported that the other two were submitted, but they are not logged. Three October packages were prepared the same way; their submission is not recorded. No award outcome for any entry is in the record.
experiments.lesson: Before automating a submission, check whether the form requires a signed-in account. Keep a per-entry confirmation log that the human also fills in; otherwise the record cannot show what was submitted.

experiments.name: xsec: cross-section check of grown surfaces
experiments.question: Do numeric surface gates catch a grown surface that jumps between windings, and can a cross-section view catch it instead?
experiments.method: Draw the grown tifxyz surface on four raw-CT slices through its height range, from a local zarr or from s3. Compare with the radial-normal gate and an on-papyrus fraction, on a public crushed scroll and on synthetic cylinders and shells.
experiments.public_summary: Published as part of the October package: 3/3 tests pass on a fresh clone, and the reproduce script was checked against the public bucket. A 2 x 2 cm patch grown with normal grids passed every numeric bar: median |cos| 0.928, 75 % of normals above 0.8, and 0.90 mm per cm of radial spread. Its cross-section still showed it jumping to the neighbouring layer at every crack. An automated on-papyrus fraction did not separate good from jumped surfaces: 0.676 vs 0.676, and 0.628 for a cross-winding surface. Submission is not recorded.
experiments.lesson: A surface that has jumped windings still faces outward, so normal-direction gates pass it. Before trusting any render or ink map built on an auto-grown surface, inspect cross-sections or use an identity measure.

experiments.name: ringstrip: patch-to-strip unrolling
experiments.question: Can many small grown patches of one winding be placed into one continuous unrolled strip, so that patch-wise ink maps can be read as a sheet?
experiments.method: Every patch pixel is placed at its azimuth about the scroll axis (times a reference radius) and its height. Overlaps are averaged, small holes are closed and seams are recorded. Tested on synthetic cylinder patches and on five real patches.
experiments.public_summary: Published as part of the October package: 2/2 tests pass on a fresh clone, and the reproduce script was checked. It unrolled five real patches into one 10,513 x 2,507 px strip. The ink map on that strip is uniform speckle; the package states this is a property of the surfaces and models, not of the tool. In synthetic tests, a line stays continuous across a seam over more than 90 % of its length, and three overlapping tiles reassemble to within 2 grey levels. Submission is not recorded.
experiments.lesson: The stitching works mechanically, but a strip is only as good as the surfaces under it. Validate surface identity (see xsec) before stitching ink maps.

experiments.name: orgsec-ink (package orgseg-ink): public ink models on organizer sheets
experiments.question: Run on CPU on segments the organizers published for two eligible scrolls, do the two public Herculaneum ink models produce maps that agree with each other or show text structure?
experiments.method: The public 9 um ink model (both layer orders) and the 2023 Grand Prize model were run on 26 organizer sheets. Agreement was measured as the Pearson r of 0.5 mm-smoothed maps, against rotated and flipped controls. A row-periodicity score was calibrated on 112 known-text tiles against 144 cross-winding junk tiles.
experiments.public_summary: Published as a package that reports nulls. Across 26 organizer sheets, the fraction of each 9 um map above 0.5 was 0.012-0.158, no pixel exceeded 0.90, and the 1-3 mm blobs showed no row alignment. Forward and reverse layer orders were unrelated. On the published agreement test the two models' maps correlated at only r = 0.13, against 0.10 for the best rotation/flip control: they do not agree. The row-periodicity score is not a text detector: only 1.8 % of known-text tiles beat the junk 99th percentile. Neither model produced a candidate. 3/3 tests pass, and the reproduce script was checked. Its null results are counted under First Letters (official-model screen, two-model agreement test, row-structure score calibration).
experiments.lesson: A null from off-the-shelf models on a new scroll means little unless they detect a positive control on the same type of scan. Publish calibration nulls, such as row periodicity failing on known text, so that nobody reuses a non-detector.

experiments.name: Blind-reader harness (local)
experiments.question: Can LLM readers be run blind and audited by code, so that no answer reaches the orchestrator and image geometry is preserved?
experiments.method: Readers see only images with random UUID names and stripped metadata. A transcript audit voids any tool call beyond reads of the listed images, one age-encrypted answer write and a DONE hand-back. Synthetic tests covered decoy files (a planted-file test), coordinate fidelity at two image sizes, and the sealed-output mode.
experiments.public_summary: The planted-file test was valid: the reader opened no decoy. The coordinate test showed that the harness silently resamples images larger than 1068 px. At 2136 px the median centre error was 57.5 px with a fitted scale of 0.966/0.964, against 0.7 px at 1068 px, so every display was capped at 1068 px per side. A read-only agent type could not write sealed answers. General-purpose agents in sealed-output mode passed the audit with 12/12 correct synthetic answers. The local job ledger records 197 jobs between 24 and 26 September (191 reads, 3 pickers, 3 sealers), all audit-valid. Disclosed residual risk: separation from the key holder is procedural and audited, not enforced by the OS.
experiments.lesson: Measure the harness on synthetic images with known geometry before any real read: the hidden resampling would have corrupted every large display. A code audit of transcripts makes it safe to use a more capable agent type.

experiments.name: Remote blind-reader harness
experiments.question: Can blind reads run in sibling containers while the answers stay sealed to a key that only the orchestrator holds, with commit order and transcripts verifiable afterwards?
experiments.method: Commit A (keys, jobs, briefs, image manifest) is pushed before any reader runs. Readers write age-sealed answers. Commit B carries the sealed files, audits and gzipped transcripts. A verifier script (rh_verify.py) checks 12 items, including that commit A precedes every answer and that each brief was used verbatim.
experiments.public_summary: This harness was declared because the main container had about 109 MB of disk free. The verifier had a normalisation bug: a batch's partial last session never matched the reference brief. It was fixed under a new code hash before any affected answer was decrypted, and the earlier batch still verified 12/12.
experiments.lesson: Commit-before-read ordering plus a scripted verifier makes remote blind reads auditable. Regression-test the verifier on batch-size edge cases, such as a partial final session.

experiments.name: Seal-key and view bookkeeping
experiments.question: Is every decryption of a sealed answer and every image view logged, so that blindness can be audited?
experiments.method: Answers are decrypted only through a logging scorer function, which appends a row (time, purpose, sealed path, sha256) to key_reads.tsv. Every image view, by a human or an agent, is appended to views.tsv with its hash and purpose.
experiments.public_summary: The decryption log holds 1,938 logged decryptions of 713 distinct sealed files, made between 24 September and 2 October, mostly for scoring, consistency checks and audits. The view log holds 22 rows: 21 owner views from a human-review set of raw CT overviews, and 1 orchestrator view of a synthetic font chart (not scroll data). The human-review set was cancelled after its first batch. The seal key lived only in the ephemeral container, and STATE records that seals would be lost if the container were reclaimed before scoring.
experiments.lesson: Route all decryption through one logging function, and keep views in their own ledger. Store the key outside the ephemeral container (a persistent secret) so that seals survive restarts; the project left this to the owner as optional.

experiments.name: Compute ledger and hardware
experiments.question: What compute did the programme use, and was it ledgered?

experiments.name: PHerc0841 known-text bank
experiments.question: Can a known-text benchmark bank be built on one scroll, with the 2.4 um reference ink mapped onto the 9 um canvas accurately enough for sealed reading tests?
experiments.method: Fetched the organizer meshes, surface volumes and 2.4 um reference slices, and mapped 2.403 -> 9.366 um by a separable area average. The mapping was validated on synthetic data and by cross-resolution NCC at small shifts. Also measured: the text area outside the exclusion shell, and whether blank windows exist. Every file is hashed in a manifest; no image was viewed.
experiments.public_summary: Built: 4,147 files (3.67 GB) with a hashed manifest. The mapping error on a synthetic test was 0.012 px, and cross-resolution NCC put the real reference mapping within ~1.4 px. The mesh grids imply a 0.37 px offset from the declared formula; this was judged negligible and disclosed. The scroll had no usable blank windows, so blanks were taken from a different known-text scroll. Reference text outside the exclusion shell was 0.248 cm2, below the 0.5 cm2 needed, so the text-order decision was pooled over all benchmark windows. Whether two segments are the same sheet was disputed and recorded as unresolved.
experiments.lesson: Build the benchmark bank first, and record every contradiction (offsets, label semantics) as a numbered correction. Here they changed two downstream design choices, the blank source and the pooled order, before any read happened.

experiments.name: Window render pipeline smoke test
experiments.question: Does the window pipeline (levelling, orientation, official renderer, alignment gate) reproduce the organizer surface volume and handle the mirror convention correctly?
experiments.method: One 1068 px window on a known-text segment was levelled and rendered with the official renderer from remote zarr. experiments.name: Data offload to a git data branch
experiments.question: Can bulk outputs be moved off a nearly full disk into a private git branch, with round-trip integrity verified before any local deletion?
experiments.method: One commit per batch, whose tree holds only that batch, built from a blob-free shallow fetch. Files are refused on size, extension, key material or symlinks. The remote tip is verified before any local removal, and every file's sha256 goes into a manifest. A synthetic round-trip self-test ran first. Pushing to the branch and deleting files each needed the owner's explicit approval.
experiments.public_summary: The self-test passed: a synthetic array was pushed, deleted locally and fetched back with an identical sha256 and equal values. After the owner's approval, 3 batches of closed-decision data (1,323 files, 3.39 GB) were offloaded, each with a verified remote tip and per-file hashes. Before that approval, the agent's safety check refused to delete a regenerable 4.9 GB docker image store. Free disk stayed near 109 MB until the owner approved the deletion, which freed about 5 GB.
experiments.lesson: Use git as cold storage only with per-batch verification and hard limits on size and file type, and get explicit approval for pushes and deletions up front. The disk crisis cost most of a day and forced reads onto remote containers.

experiments.name: Sibling fleet operation
experiments.question: How large did the fleet of sibling sessions grow, how was it coordinated, and how did it stop?
experiments.method: Builder/trainer sibling cloud sessions, each on its own branch, with no access to seals, scoring or viewing. Orders went out by one-shot triggers, decision requests came back through ASK.md, and each sibling kept a RESUME.md. The fleet grew in waves from 25 September. On 9 October an owner standing order asked for the maximum fleet at all times, with every sibling running a declared, measurable job.
experiments.public_summary: The registry lists 118 sibling sessions created between 25 September and 2 October, on 95 branches (94 of them sib-* worker branches plus fl4t). Another 22 sib-* branches are not in the registry (sub-siblings and other worker lanes started outside the registry, among them one First Letters lane and a checkpoint branch), giving 116 sib-* worker branches. A further fleet of 52 sessions started on 9 October for umbilicus, ink-model and survey lanes. On 9 October it was found that idle containers are reclaimed after a turn ends and their detached jobs die, so the effective fleet had been a fraction of the session count. Earlier, on 2 October, every lane's keepalive had overrun the 7,200 s background limit and been killed; the lanes stopped because the harness forbade restarting the command. At about 05:15Z on 10 October every sibling session stopped with 'out of usage credits' (a seven-day limit), and the remaining survey work ran locally.
experiments.lesson: Session count is not compute. Make jobs resumable, keep each turn alive within known background-time limits, and budget the account's usage before scaling out. A fleet that outgrows its usage budget stops all at once.

experiments.name: Keepalive dispatch protocol
experiments.question: Can a dispatcher sibling send resumable, keep-alive job orders to the whole fleet from a committed brief?
experiments.method: SIB-KEEPALIVE-1: job scripts are resumable and write DONE markers; siblings poll in calls of under 10 minutes until DONE; backup triggers fire 100 minutes later. A dispatcher sibling was to create the 72 triggers from logs/sib/dispatch_2026-10-09_2300.md.
experiments.public_summary: The dispatcher created 0 of 72 triggers. Its permission classifier refused both the plan script and the first trigger, treating orders that tell sessions to keep themselves alive with detached jobs as creating unsafe agents. The dispatcher did not rephrase the orders to get around the refusal. The orchestrator created 12 re-run triggers itself, and the 24-lane second pass was never dispatched. A later survey order went to 24 lanes, but only 17 of 72 positions, from 8 lanes, finished before usage credits ran out.
experiments.lesson: To a permission layer, orders that tell other sessions to keep themselves alive look like creating unsafe agents. Agree the orchestration pattern and its permissions before scaling, or run the compute without AI turns, as the later fleet did.

experiments.name: Multi-agent prompt regeneration
experiments.question: Can a multi-agent workflow regenerate the master prompt after each context condensation without losing integrity rules?
experiments.method: After a condensation, a workflow of 24 agents drafted, critiqued and verified a new master prompt. Under the compute-economy order it was limited to one run per 24 hours.
experiments.public_summary: The v8 run used 1,454,186 subagent tokens across 24 agents, and only 3 completed. The account usage limit killed it, and the run itself helped hit that limit. It was retired. Its replacement is a single-pass refresh at most once per 24 hours, with a scripted diff that checks every integrity rule is kept verbatim, plus a live handover file that is read first after every restart.
experiments.lesson: Large self-maintenance workflows draw on the same usage budget as the research. A small, maintained handover file plus a scripted integrity diff was cheaper and enough.

experiments.name: Append-only decision log integrity
experiments.question: Is the hash-chained declaration log intact, so that declarations demonstrably precede results?
experiments.method: Each RULES.md entry carries the sha256 of the previous entry, and the project verifier recomputes the chain. VERIFY.md documents one-command checks for code hashes and for re-scoring. The survey re-ran the verifier read-only.
experiments.public_summary: The project's chain verifier, re-run at survey time, returned OK on all 397 entries, from 24 September to the last result on 10 October. The ledger of decision verdicts (LEDGER.md) holds 12 rows, most with scorer-output hashes. None concerns this family: tools and operations were recorded as declarations and results in the chained log, not as ledger verdicts.
experiments.lesson: A hash-chained, append-only log plus per-result code hashes is cheap and lets outsiders verify the ordering after the fact. Keep it running even when everything else is failing.

families.summary: Besides its research questions, Dominion built and released tools. It also ran a blind-reader harness with a decryption and view audit trail, offloaded data from a nearly full disk to a git data branch, and ran a fleet of sibling sessions: 118 registered between 25 September and 2 October and 52 more on 9 October. Six standalone tools were published for the monthly Progress Prizes, three in September and three in October; each passed clean-clone tests and a leak scrub. The log confirms one September entry as submitted, and the prize outcome is not in the record. The main costs were usage limits, container reclaims, background-time limits and permission refusals. The sibling fleet finally stopped on 2026-10-10, when the account ran out of usage credits.
